title: Given an array where each value is the maximum jump length from that index, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first. Explain the greedy farthest-reach approach, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Jump Game (Can You Reach the Last Index with a Greedy Reach)

s1_definition.profdef: Jump Game decides reachability of the last index when each index allows a jump of up to its value. The greedy approach scans left to right maintaining the farthest index reachable so far; if the current index ever exceeds that reach, we are stuck and return false, otherwise we extend the reach and succeed once it covers the last index. It runs in a single linear pass.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India plans a multi-leg fund transfer where each account permits forwarding up to a certain number of legs ahead, and we check whether the funds can reach the final settlement account.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track the farthest reachable index; if an index passes it, you are stuck.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Jump Game decides reachability of the last index when each index allows a jump of up to its value. The greedy approach scans left to right maintaining the farthest index reachable so far; if the current index ever exceeds that reach, we are stuck and return false, otherwise we extend the reach and succeed once it covers the last index. It runs in a single linear pass.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India plans a multi-leg fund transfer where each account permits forwarding up to a certain number of legs ahead, and we check whether the funds can reach the final settlement account.

**One line to remember:** Track the farthest reachable index; if an index passes it, you are stuck.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a single variable, the farthest index we can currently reach, starting at zero. We scan each index from left to right. If the current index is beyond the farthest reach, there is no way to have arrived here, so we return false. Otherwise we update the farthest reach to the maximum of itself and the current index plus its jump value. The moment the farthest reach covers or passes the last index, we can stop and return true.

The core scan is `int farthest = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (i > farthest) return false; farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]); if (farthest >= n - 1) return true; } return true;`. A concrete check: with jumps 2, 3, 1, 1, 4 we reach the end, while with 3, 2, 1, 0, 4 we get stuck at the zero before the last index and return false. Senior nuance: the greedy works because reachability is monotone, so the farthest reach fully summarises the past; it is linear time and constant space, far better than a quadratic dynamic programming over every pair of indices.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India plans a chained fund transfer across a sequence of intermediary accounts, where each account can forward the funds up to a certain number of accounts ahead based on its clearing limit, and the operations team wants to know whether the funds can reach the final settlement account. Trying every forwarding combination is exponential. This is exactly how Jump Game works: greedily track the farthest account reachable and detect a dead end.

The code defines a `TransferReachService` with `canReachFinal(limits)` using the farthest-reach scan. A `Demo` provides forwarding limits and logs whether the final account is reachable.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is forwarding limits two, three, one, one, four across five accounts indexed zero to four. Step 1: the farthest reach starts at zero. Step 2: at account zero, zero is within reach, and account zero can forward two ahead, so the reach extends to two. Step 3: at account one, one is within the reach of two, and it can forward three ahead, so the reach extends to four. Step 4: four is the last index, so the reach now covers the final account and we return true immediately. Had an account had a limit of zero sitting just before the end, the scan would find a later index exceeding the farthest reach and return false, signalling a dead end.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:51:25 PM com.bank.txreach.service.TransferReachService canReachFinal
INFO: Final settlement account is reachable
Oct 27, 2026 9:51:25 PM com.bank.txreach.TransferReachApplication main
INFO: Can reach final settlement account = true
```

```
    │

  farthest = 0
    ▼ i=0 (0<=0)  farthest = max(0, 0+2) = 2
    ▼ i=1 (1<=2)  farthest = max(2, 1+3) = 4  ≥ last(4) → reachable
    │
    ▼
  Output: true

  (counter: [3,2,1,0,4] → i=3 limit0, reach stuck at 3 < 4 → false)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game asks whether I can reach the last index of an array when each index lets me jump up to its own value, and the elegant solution is a greedy scan that tracks a single number: the farthest index I can currently reach. I walk left to right, and at each index I first check whether that index is even reachable, meaning it lies within the farthest reach I have accumulated. If an index ever lies beyond that reach, there is no way to have arrived, so I immediately return false.

Otherwise I extend the farthest reach to the maximum of its current value and the current index plus its jump value, and the moment that reach covers the last index I can stop and return true. The reason the greedy is correct is that reachability is monotone: once a stretch of indices is reachable, the only thing that matters going forward is how far I can now get, which the single farthest-reach variable captures completely. This is linear time and constant space, a big improvement over a quadratic dynamic programming that checks every pair of indices.

At the National Bank of India I used this to validate a chained fund transfer across intermediary accounts, where each account could forward the funds a limited number of legs ahead based on its clearing limit, and we needed to know whether the funds could reach the final settlement account before initiating the chain. Explaining the farthest-reach invariant, the stuck condition when an index exceeds it, and why monotone reachability justifies the greedy is what shows an interviewer I can spot when a greedy beats a dynamic programming.
